hints: Hint 1: Recall the definition of isotopes in terms of proton number $Z$ which determines the element.
Hint 2: Use $A = Z + N$ to deduce what must differ if $Z$ is the same but the mass numbers are different.
teacher_walkthrough: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element with the same proton number $Z$ but different nucleon number $A$.
Same element means same $Z$, so number of protons in P equals number of protons in Q: $$Z_P = Z_Q$$
Since $A = Z + N$, different $A$ with same $Z$ requires different neutron number $N = A - Z$.
walkthrough: Mark scheme step 1: number of protons is equal / the same.
Mark scheme step 2: number of neutrons is unequal / different.
common_pitfalls: Stating that isotopes have the same number of nucleons or same mass number.
Reversing the comparison and stating protons are different and neutrons are the same.
Referring only to electrons instead of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

hints: Hint 1: Recall that $\beta^{-}$ decay is a neutron changing to a proton inside the nucleus and compare quark structures $n = udd$ and $p = uud$.
teacher_walkthrough: $\beta^{-}$ decay at nucleon level is neutron to proton conversion: $$n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}_e$$
Quark structure of neutron is $udd$ and quark structure of proton is $uud$.
Comparing $udd$ to $uud$ shows one $d$ quark changes to a $u$ quark: $$d \rightarrow u$$
walkthrough: Mark scheme step 1: down quark to up quark / $udd$ changes to $uud$.
common_pitfalls: Stating up to down which is the change for $\beta^{+}$ decay, not $\beta^{-}$ decay.
Describing proton to neutron change instead of neutron to proton change.

hints: Hint 1: Recall that $\beta^{-}$ decay must conserve lepton number and energy, so a second lepton is emitted with the electron.
teacher_walkthrough: Lepton number and energy momentum conservation in $\beta^{-}$ decay requires: $$n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}_e$$
The $e^{-}$ carries lepton number $+1$, so an antilepton with lepton number $-1$ is required to keep total lepton number zero.
This particle is the electron antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_e$.
common_pitfalls: Stating neutrino instead of antineutrino; $\beta^{-}$ emits an antineutrino while $\beta^{+}$ emits a neutrino.
Stating gamma photon, which is emitted in de-excitation but is not required for lepton conservation in beta decay.

hints: Hint 1: Recall the quark charges: charm is $+2/3e$ and bottom is $-1/3e$.
Hint 2: Set up the sum for three quarks as $Q = Q_c + Q_c + Q_b$ and combine the fractions over a common denominator.
teacher_walkthrough: Charge is additive for quarks in a hadron: $$Q_{total} = Q_c + Q_c + Q_b$$
walkthrough: Mark scheme step 1: charm = +2/3e and bottom = -1/3e / 2 x charm is +4/3e.
common_pitfalls: Using $-1/3e$ for charm or $+2/3e$ for bottom; charm is up-type (+2/3) and bottom is down-type (-1/3).
Forgetting there are two charm quarks and calculating only $2/3 - 1/3$.
Giving the answer as a decimal or in coulombs instead of in terms of $e$ as requested.
